F1.quote: Given the rapid adoption of generative AI and its potential to impact a wide range of tasks, understanding the effects of AI on the economy is one of society’s most important questions.
F1.claim: the question the work answers: the effects of AI on the economy
F1.lineage: why: the economic effects of AI

F2.quote: In this work, we take a step toward that goal by analyzing the work activities people do with AI, how successfully and broadly those activities are done, and combine that with data on what occupations do those activities.
F2.claim: what the work does: analyses the work activities people do with AI, how successfully and broadly, combined with data on which occupations do them
F2.lineage: what it is: measuring AI's applicability to occupations from real use

F3.quote: We analyze a dataset of 200k anonymized and privacy-scrubbed conversations between users and Microsoft Bing Copilot, a publicly available generative AI system.
F3.claim: the data: 200k anonymized, privacy-scrubbed conversations between users and Microsoft Bing Copilot
F3.lineage: the data: one provider's own product, Bing Copilot

F4.quote: We find the most common work activities people seek AI assistance for involve gathering information and writing, while the most common activities that AI itself is performing are providing information and assistance, writing, teaching, and advising.
F4.claim: the July 2025 finding by side: users seek help gathering information and writing; the AI provides information and assistance, writes, teaches and advises

F5.quote: Combining these activity classifications with measurements of task success and scope of impact, we compute an AI applicability score for each occupation.
F5.claim: the AI applicability score: activity classifications combined with task success and scope of impact, per occupation
F5.lineage: success measures and the AI applicability score

F6.quote: We find the highest AI applicability scores for knowledge work occupation groups such as computer and mathematical, and office and administrative support, as well as occupations such as sales whose work activities involve providing and communicating information.
F6.claim: the July 2025 headline: the highest scores for knowledge work groups (computer and mathematical; office and administrative support) and for occupations such as sales

F7.quote: Additionally, we characterize the types of work activities performed most successfully, how wage and education correlate with AI applicability, and how real-world usage compares to predictions of occupational AI impact.
F7.claim: further analyses: activities performed most successfully; wage and education against applicability; real-world usage against predictions of occupational AI impact

F8.quote: Blog & Podcasts … Applicability vs. job displacement: further notes on our recent research on AI and occupations
F8.claim: the operator's page links a note distinguishing applicability from job displacement (the note itself outside B, not fetched)
F8.lineage: the limit: applicability is not replacement

F9.quote: These describe how often Bing Copilot was used for different work activities, how successfully, and what this usage indicates about which occupations AI may be applicable to.
F9.claim: what the metrics describe: how often and how successfully Bing Copilot was used for work activities, and which occupations AI may be applicable to
F9.lineage: what it is: measuring AI's applicability to occupations from real use

F10.quote: The goal of these metrics is to measure how AI may be useful in different occupations.
F10.claim: the metrics' goal: how AI may be useful in different occupations
F10.lineage: what it is: measuring AI's applicability to occupations from real use

F11.quote: In particular, they include our metrics aggregated at the O*NET intermediate work activity (IWA) and occupation (detailed 2018 SOC code) level.
F11.claim: the unit of aggregation: O*NET intermediate work activities and detailed 2018 SOC occupations
F11.lineage: the unit: user goals and AI actions mapped to O*NET work activities and occupations

F12.quote: `iwa_metrics.csv`: IWA-level metrics, reported separately for user goals and AI actions.
F12.claim: user goals and AI actions reported separately
F12.lineage: the unit: user goals and AI actions mapped to O*NET work activities and occupations

F13.quote: `completion_{user,ai}`: the fraction of conversations mapping to an IWA (as a user goal or AI action) where our completion classfiier indicates that the LLM completed the user’s goal.
F13.claim: completion: the fraction of conversations where the completion classifier indicates the LLM completed the user's goal ('classfiier' as written)
F13.lineage: success measures and the AI applicability score

F14.locus: IWA-level metrics, impact scope and feedback
F14.quote: `impact_scope_{user,ai}`: the fraction of conversations mapping to an IWA (as a user goal or AI action) where the classified scope of impact is moderate or higher. … `feedback_positive_fraction_{user,ai}`: of all thumbs reactions in Copilot-Thumbs on conversations mapping to an IWA (as a user goal or AI action), the fraction where the reaction was a thumbs up.
F14.claim: impact scope (classified moderate or higher) and positive feedback (the thumbs-up fraction in Copilot-Thumbs)
F14.lineage: success measures and the AI applicability score

F15.quote: The two sides are averaged together to compute the final AI applicability scores reported in `ai_applicability_scores.csv`.
F15.claim: the score: the user-goal side and the AI-action side averaged
F15.lineage: success measures and the AI applicability score

F16.quote: (current) v1.1: referenced by the NeurIPS '26 version and by arXiv paper revisions v6 and v7. Adds physical task classification, nonphysical IWA weights, and nonphysical AI applicability score.
F16.claim: results v1.1, referenced by the NeurIPS 2026 version and arXiv v6–v7, adding physical-task classification and nonphysical weights and score

F17.quote: This leaves us with 785 SOC codes covering 149.8 million workers according to the 2023 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) data (total US employment in 2023 OEWS data is 151.9 million).
F17.claim: coverage of occupations: 785 SOC codes, 149.8 million of 151.9 million US workers (2023 OEWS)

F18.quote: The conversations contributing to these results are from Bing Copilot in the United States from January 1, 2024 to September 30, 2024, so may not represent AI usage in other countries.
F18.claim: the window and its limit: Bing Copilot in the US, 1 January to 30 September 2024, so may not represent other countries

F19.quote: Our metrics should not be misconstrued or misrepresented as measuring the ability of AI to replace jobs.
F19.claim: the stated limit: the metrics do not measure the ability of AI to replace jobs
F19.lineage: the limit: applicability is not replacement

F20.quote: There is more to an occupation than the sum of its O*NET tasks, and our measures of success (completion, scope, and thumbs feedback) are proxies that do not capture full workplace capabilities.
F20.claim: an occupation is more than its tasks; completion, scope and thumbs feedback are proxies

F21.quote: Rather, our metrics indicate (1) what a consumer LLM is used for, (2) in a relative sense, which of these uses are more or less successful, and (3) which occupations may find AI more useful or applicable as a result.
F21.claim: what the metrics indicate instead: what a consumer LLM is used for; relative success; which occupations may find AI more applicable
F21.lineage: what it is: measuring AI's applicability to occupations from real use

F22.quote: These results were computed from Bing Copilot conversation data, which was originally collected by Microsoft and consists of conversations between users and Bing Copilot.
F22.claim: the data were collected by Microsoft from its own product's users
F22.lineage: the data: one provider's own product, Bing Copilot

F23.quote: The classification of conversations into IWAs was performed by an LLM pipeline designed by Kiran Tomlinson, Siddharth Suri, and Scott Counts.
F23.claim: the classification was performed by an LLM pipeline the authors designed
F23.lineage: the pipeline: an LLM classifier and its limit

F24.quote: LLM-based classifiers are imperfect, so all metrics should be interpreted with caution. See the paper for the exact prompts we used and for interrater reliability with human annotators.
F24.claim: the classifier's limit: imperfect, metrics to be read with caution; prompts and interrater reliability in the paper
F24.lineage: the pipeline: an LLM classifier and its limit

F25.quote: As these results are based on consumer AI usage, they do not represent the full distribution of AI use in the workplace. For some work tasks, AI tools are directly integrated into specialized software, or specific models are used for their dedicated capability or compliance with data security requirements.
F25.claim: consumer use does not represent workplace AI use, where tools are integrated into specialized software or chosen for capability or compliance

F26.quote: The majority of conversations were in English, but we did not filter by language.

F27.quote: Data analysis was conducted with approval from the Microsoft Institutional Review Board.
F27.claim: approval by the Microsoft Institutional Review Board

F28.quote: This research was conducted by members of [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/).
F28.claim: the operator: members of Microsoft Research

F29.quote: This repository is licensed under CC BY 4.0.

F30.quote: With generative AI emerging as a general-purpose technology, understanding its economic effects is among society's most pressing questions.
F30.claim: the question, in v7's words: the economic effects of a general-purpose technology
F30.lineage: why: the economic effects of AI

F31.quote: Earlier work on AI impact largely relied on predictions of AI capabilities or focused narrowly on individual firms. Drawing instead on real-world AI usage, we analyze a dataset of 200k anonymized conversations with Microsoft Bing Copilot to measure AI applicability to occupations.
F31.claim: the definition by contrast: measured from real-world usage (200k Bing Copilot conversations), against earlier work's predictions of capability or single-firm studies
F31.lineage: what it is: measuring AI's applicability to occupations from real use

F32.quote: We use an LLM-based pipeline to classify the O*NET work activities assisted or performed by AI in each conversation.
F32.claim: the pipeline classifies the O*NET work activities assisted or performed by AI in each conversation
F32.lineage: the pipeline: an LLM classifier and its limit

F33.quote: We find that the most common and successful AI-assisted work activities involve information work--the creation, processing, and communication of information.
F33.claim: headline finding (v7): the most common and successful AI-assisted activities are information work

F34.quote: At the occupation level, we find widespread AI applicability cutting across sectors, as most occupations have information work components.
F34.claim: at the occupation level, applicability cuts across sectors

F35.quote: Our methodology also allows us to predict which occupations are more likely to delegate tasks to AI and which are more likely to use AI to assist existing workflows.
F35.claim: the method predicts which occupations are more likely to delegate tasks to AI and which to use AI to assist existing workflows

F36.quote: Finally, we see an increase in occupation-level AI applicability over our 9-month data period, driven primarily by people using AI for more varied tasks.
F36.claim: applicability rose over the nine months, driven mainly by more varied tasks
